rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to determine whether the two critical pairs respond to a shallower slope. The initial last-peak time suggests this should spread the crowded region while keeping the final peak near 10 minutes.

Shift the starting composition upward while preserving almost the same gradient slope as the fully resolved second run. This should remove low-organic waiting time, bring the last peak below 10 minutes, and retain adequate resolution of the critical pair.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to lift the remaining critical pair above R = 1.5. Based on the previous slope response, the last peak should remain close to the 10-minute threshold, potentially reaching the maximum CRF.

Raise the starting organic fraction to bring the last peak clearly below 10 minutes, eliminating the small time penalty hidden by score rounding. Keeping the endpoint and duration fixed also makes the gradient slightly shallower, which should help preserve critical-pair resolution.

Injection 5 reaches the maximum CRF; now test a 5 °C temperature increase to shorten retention while checking critical-pair selectivity. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate the temperature effect, retaining injection 5 as the fully resolved benchmark.

The critical pair converged sharply at 45 °C; test 55 °C to see whether it separates again after an elution-order reversal. This could provide a faster fully resolved method, though the other middle peaks also need monitoring.

Slightly lengthen the gradient at 55 °C to try to resolve the new critical pair while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. This also tests whether the temperature-separated neighboring pair retains sufficient resolution as the slope decreases.

Use a gradient slope between injections 7 and 8 to shorten the fully resolved 55 °C method. Interpolating their responses suggests both critical pairs should remain above R = 1.5, with the last peak around 9 minutes.

Shift both gradient endpoints upward by 0.05, preserving injection 9’s slope while reducing initial retention time. Check whether the early peaks remain sufficiently retained and the two critical middle pairs stay resolved.

Lower the starting organic fraction to protect the early peaks and improve the middle pair that deteriorated in injection 10, while steepening the gradient to shorten late retention. This tests whether the starting-composition benefit permits a faster fully resolved method than injection 9.

Shorten injection 11’s gradient by one grid step to test the fastest fully resolved boundary at 55 °C. The steeper slope may improve the close pair at rows 6–7, but the pair at rows 4–5 must remain above R = 1.5.

Reduce the endpoint to give a slope between injections 11 and 12, aiming to restore the critical pair above R = 1.5. This should retain full resolution while bringing the last peak out slightly earlier than injection 11.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 13 while keeping the endpoint safely above the observed elution window. The measured slope response predicts the critical pairs will remain just above R = 1.5, with the last peak near 7.8 minutes.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction improves middle-pair selectivity enough to tolerate a steeper gradient than injection 14. This explores a potentially faster fully resolved method while retaining the established maximum-CRF methods as benchmarks.

With maximum CRF secured, test a substantially faster gradient at 60 °C for a new selectivity regime. The critical middle pair may separate after reversing order, while the low starting composition protects early retention.

Test whether raising the starting organic fraction separates the middle pair on the opposite side of its apparent order reversal at 60 °C. This could retain the short elution time of injection 16, but early-peak resolution and the neighboring middle pair need checking.

Shorten only the gradient to measure the slope response of the unresolved pair in the fast 60 °C regime. A steeper gradient may improve its separation after the apparent order reversal, although the neighboring pair at R = 1.62 could become limiting.

The fast 60 °C methods remain limited by competing middle-pair separations, so test the unexplored low-temperature selectivity regime. A broad 10-minute gradient should keep all compounds observable while revealing whether reordered pairs permit another fully resolved, short method.

Return to the fastest fully resolved benchmark, injection 15, and shorten its gradient by one grid step. This directly tests the speed boundary at 55 °C while retaining injection 15 as a maximum-CRF fallback.

Test 35 °C as an intermediate selectivity regime that may separate the crowded peaks without the long gradient required at 40 °C. The broad endpoint limits late retention, while established maximum-CRF methods remain available if another pair becomes limiting.

Trim injection 15’s unused high-organic gradient tail while preserving its starting composition and slope exactly. The last peak previously eluted near 0.57 organic, so this endpoint should preserve full resolution and the 7.6-minute last-peak time with a shorter programmed gradient.

With the maximum CRF secured, refine a method with more resolution margin than the fastest benchmark. This slope lies between injections 8 and 9 and should keep both critical pairs above 1.5 with the last peak below 10 minutes.

Use a slope between injections 8 and 23 to balance their two limiting pairs, targeting a minimum resolution near 1.7. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, preserving maximum CRF with more resolution margin than the fastest methods.

Trim injection 24’s unused high-organic tail and slightly steepen its gradient, targeting full resolution with the last peak around 9.3 minutes. The endpoint remains above the observed last-peak elution composition, so all peaks should stay within the gradient while preserving maximum CRF.
